title: How Much Does Attic Insulation Cost?
h1: How Much Does Attic Insulation Cost? What Shapes the Estimate
description: Attic insulation cost depends on attic size, material, target depth, access and whether old insulation is removed first. Here is what goes into an estimate.
quick_answer: Attic insulation cost depends on the size of the attic, the type of insulation, how deep it needs to be, how easy the attic is to work in, whether old insulation has to be removed and whether air sealing is done first. Blown-in insulation added over clean existing material is usually the simplest job.
body:
Adding or replacing attic insulation is one of the more straightforward home improvements, but the price can still vary quite a bit. The size of your attic is only part of it. The material, the depth, the condition of what's there now and the prep work all play a role.

What goes into the cost of attic insulation?

Attic size

Insulation is priced by area and depth, so a bigger attic means more material and more labor. For most homes, the attic area is close to the footprint of the top floor.

Type of insulation

The two most common types in Southern California homes are blown-in (loose fill) and batts. Blown-in fiberglass and cellulose fill gaps and irregular spaces well and go in quickly. Batts work well in open joist bays with standard spacing. Spray foam is another option but is used less often in existing attics and costs more.

Target R-value and depth

R-value measures how well insulation slows heat flow. Higher R-value means more material, and for blown-in insulation that means more depth. Many older homes have far less insulation than current recommendations, so bringing them up to a modern level takes more material.

Removing old insulation

If the existing insulation is clean and dry, new insulation can often be added on top. If it's contaminated by rodents, water-damaged, moldy or badly compressed, it should come out first. Removal adds labor, equipment and disposal.

Air sealing

Gaps around light fixtures, wiring, plumbing, top plates and the attic hatch let air move between the house and the attic. Sealing them before insulating makes the insulation work better. It adds some cost but is usually worth it.

Access and obstacles

A small hatch, low roof pitch, HVAC equipment, ductwork or stored items in the attic all slow the job down. Recessed lights may need covers or clearances, depending on their rating.

Blown-in or batts: which costs less?

It depends on the attic. Blown-in insulation is usually faster to install over large or irregular areas and fills around obstacles well. Batts can make sense for small, open attics or for DIY projects. For most existing homes with a typical attic, blown-in is the common choice. The right answer for your home comes down to the space, the existing insulation and the depth you need.

Does attic insulation pay for itself?

It can. A well-insulated attic slows the heat that pours through the ceiling on hot afternoons and the warmth that escapes on cool nights. That means your AC and furnace run less. How much you save depends on how much insulation you have now, how much you use heating and cooling, and the condition of your ducts. Homes with very little insulation and ducts in the attic usually see the biggest difference, especially inland.

Can you install attic insulation yourself?

Some homeowners lay batts in an easy, open attic on their own. Blown-in insulation needs a blowing machine and a second person, and getting an even depth across the whole attic takes practice. Any DIY job also needs care around recessed lights, wiring and soffit vents, and it shouldn't be attempted over insulation with rodent droppings or water damage. If the attic needs cleaning or air sealing, that's usually where a professional crew earns its keep.

Are there rebates or incentives?

Utility and government programs for insulation and air sealing change over time, and eligibility rules vary. Ask about current programs when you get your estimate. You can also check our current specials for discounts we're running.

What should you look for in an estimate?

  • The type of insulation and the target R-value or depth.
  • Whether old insulation is removed or left in place.
  • Whether air sealing is included and which areas it covers.
  • How recessed lights, the attic hatch and vents will be handled.
  • Baffles to keep insulation from blocking soffit vents, if your attic has them.
  • Cleanup and disposal.

Comparing these items line by line is more useful than comparing totals.

For an accurate number, we'll measure the attic, check the existing insulation and look for air leaks, pest activity and moisture before recommending a material and depth. Learn more about our attic insulation service. Estimates are free.
faqs: Can new insulation go on top of old insulation?
Yes, if the old insulation is dry, clean and free of rodent contamination or mold. Contaminated or water-damaged insulation should be removed first.
How long does it take to install attic insulation?
Blowing in new insulation over existing material often takes a few hours. Jobs that include removal, cleaning and air sealing usually take longer, sometimes a full day or more.
Is blown-in insulation cheaper than batts?

It depends on the attic. Blown-in insulation is often faster to install in typical attics with obstacles and irregular spaces, which can keep labor down. An estimate for your attic will show the real difference.
What R-value should my attic have?
It depends on your home and the current recommendations for your area. Many older homes fall well short of modern levels. We can measure what you have and recommend a target.
